answer:
I can't tell you yet whether the edge state survives on real hardware. As you asked, the final job ran on garnet:mock and not on the real QPU. The mock returns made-up counts that ignore the circuit, so those numbers say nothing about the physics.

What I ran: I built two 8-site SSH chains with H = sum b (XX+YY)/2. One chain starts with a weak bond at the end (weak, strong, weak and so on, b = 0.3 and 1.0). The other starts with a strong bond. In both, one electron starts on the end site. Each chain evolves to time t = 2 in 4 Trotter steps. The chain sits on Garnet qubits QB1, QB2, QB5, QB4, QB3, QB8, QB9 and QB10, and the end site is QB1. The server received 56 CZ gates per circuit, with all 8 qubits measured. First I sent a 100-shot test job (01a1609d-4608-711e-a944-fbd118005fe7). The final job (01a1609d-b14d-73d9-981d-8354dfd6eca5) sent both circuits together with 1000 shots each. The API reported 1.0 billed second for that job. Mock jobs cost 0 credits.

Ideal results (noiseless simulation of the circuits I submitted):
- Weak-bond-first chain: the electron stays on the end site with probability 0.763. The exact physics model gives 0.767.
- Strong-bond-first chain: the probability drops to 0.144. The exact model gives 0.142.
- In both circuits, every ideal shot holds exactly one electron.

Mock results: the end qubit read 1 in 0.504 of shots for the weak-bond-first chain and 0.497 for the other. About 13% of shots held exactly one 1 (0.128 and 0.126). None of those single-1 shots had the 1 on the end site, so the postselected edge probability is 0.0 for both. These numbers are close to coin flips, and the two chains look the same. That is what a mock returns.

What it shows: in theory, the end of a weak-bond-first chain traps the electron in a protected edge state, so it stays put about 5 times more often than on a strong-bond-first chain. A real Garnet run of these same two circuits would test whether that gap survives hardware noise. Each circuit has 56 CZ gates, so noise will shrink the gap. The single-electron share and the postselected edge probability would show how much.

For polyacetylene: the SSH model predicts that a chain that ends on a weak bond holds a localized electron state at its end. In the real plastic, the same thing happens at defects where the bond pattern flips. These are solitons, and they help explain why doped polyacetylene conducts. This run checks the circuit and the theory numbers. It does not test the real material or real hardware. Counts are in Qiskit order, so the rightmost bit is the end site. The script is at /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_dd9c267c-1c6-3/ssh_run.py, and the job IDs are in /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_dd9c267c-1c6-3/job_log.txt.
